subject: pluto-dwarf-planet
title: Pluto and the Problem of Defining a Planet
summary: Why the IAU's 2006 definition demoted Pluto, what it optimizes for, and where critics say it breaks.

keys.prompt: What do the IAU's three planet criteria test, and which one does Pluto fail?
keys.answer: Orbiting the Sun, enough mass to be round (hydrostatic equilibrium), and clearing its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto fails the third.

keys.prompt: What trade-off did the 'cleared the neighbourhood' criterion resolve?
keys.answer: A shape-only rule would add many planets (Brown estimated 53, likely 200+ eventually); a dominance rule keeps the list to eight.

keys.prompt: What are the strongest criticisms of the 2006 definition?
keys.answer: Few voted (424 of ~9,000), no planet fully clears its orbit, and the test depends on location, so a Mars-sized body far out would fail it.

cards.title: Same object, new category
cards.text: Nothing about Pluto changed on 24 August 2006. What changed was the word. Astronomers voted on a formal definition of 'planet', and the solar system went from nine to eight. Definitions are models: they buy clarity at the cost of edge cases.

cards.question: The IAU had about 9,000 members in 2006. What share do you think were present for the vote that demoted Pluto?
cards.reveal: About 4.7%: 424 astronomers, less than 5% of the community, on the last day of a 10-day meeting.

cards.title: Discovery forces definition
cards.text: This is a rerun. Ceres, found in 1801, was hailed as the missing planet; by 1851 there were 23 'planets' and astronomers split off the asteroids. Pluto's turn came in stages: Charon's discovery in 1978 let astronomers weigh Pluto at roughly 1/25 of Mercury's mass, smaller than our Moon. Then Quaoar, Sedna and Eris showed Pluto had peers.
cards.example: In 2006 Eris was briefly measured as larger than Pluto. Either it was the tenth planet, or neither was a planet.

why.q: Why did more discoveries make a definition unavoidable rather than optional?
why.a: Without one, every new Pluto-sized find raised the planet count ad hoc; astronomers expected many more and also worried about classifying planets around other stars.

cards.title: Shape vs. dominance
cards.text: The IAU's 16 August draft was purely physical: round and orbiting a star. That would have added Ceres, Eris and Charon (as a double planet with Pluto), with a dozen more candidates. Mike Brown estimated at least 53 known bodies would qualify, probably over 200 eventually. The final rule added a dynamical test: a planet must have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
cards.example: Trade-off: a shape rule describes the body; a dominance rule describes its role in the system and keeps the list short.

cards.title: Legitimacy of the vote
cards.text: Voting in Prague was by raised yellow cards. Only 424 astronomers attended, under 5% of roughly 9,000 members, on the last day after many had left. The Pluto resolution passed 237–157 with 30 abstentions. Defenders note a representative sample of 400 from 9,000 is statistically adequate, and that only planetary specialists really needed to weigh in.
cards.example: The objection is about selection, not sample size: who stays for the last day is not a random draw.

cards.title: Is 'cleared' coherent?
cards.text: Alan Stern, New Horizons' lead scientist, argues no planet has cleared its zone: Earth orbits with about 10,000 near-Earth asteroids, Jupiter with 100,000 Trojans. "If Neptune had cleared its zone, Pluto wouldn't be there." The rebuttal: planets dominate, not empty, their zones. Neptune long ago locked Pluto into a 3:2 resonance, so Neptune sets Pluto's orbit.
cards.example: Read 'cleared' as 'gravitationally controls' and the eight pass cleanly; read it literally and none do.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: The test depends on location: a Mars-sized body in the inner Oort cloud could not clear so large a zone and would fail. Mercury is not actually in hydrostatic equilibrium yet is explicitly a planet. And the text says 'Sun', so it does not cover planets of other stars, where a separate working definition applies.
cards.example: A good definition is judged by usefulness, not by whether it is ever awkward.

cards.question: Is a definition that is useful but has awkward edge cases better than one that is consistent but makes the category huge? Make the strongest case for the side you'd vote against.
nudges: Where else do you draw a bright line knowing it misclassifies a few cases?
Who should get a vote on a scientific definition?

questions.q: A newly found body orbits the Sun, is round, and shares its orbit with many similar objects it does not control. Under the IAU rule it is:

options.why: Right. It passes the first two tests but not clearing its neighbourhood.
It fails criterion (c): it hasn't cleared or come to dominate its orbit.
That category is for bodies that are not round; this one is.
Satellites orbit planets; this orbits the Sun.

questions.q: What was the main practical effect of adding the dynamical (clearing) criterion?

options.text: It kept the planet count at eight instead of a list that could grow into the dozens or hundreds
options.why: Yes. A shape-only rule would have admitted Ceres, Eris, Charon and many more.

options.text: It made Pluto a planet again
options.why: The opposite: it is the criterion Pluto fails.

options.text: It fixed the definition for exoplanets
options.why: The text says 'Sun', so it does not cover other stars' planets.

options.text: It removed Mercury from the list
options.why: Mercury is explicitly included despite not being in hydrostatic equilibrium.

questions.q: Which is the strongest counter to Stern's 'Earth hasn't cleared its orbit either' argument?

options.text: Planets gravitationally dominate their zones, e.g. Neptune controls Pluto's orbit via a 3:2 resonance
options.why: Right. On this reading, 'cleared' means control, not emptiness.
They do; there are about 10,000 of them.
That's a critique of the process, not a reply to Stern's physics.
Trojans orbit the Sun along Jupiter's path; they aren't its moons.
